Wiktor Tomasik — One reader, many histories

Current research in The Mind in the Mirror: Self-Models at https://pixedar.github.io/.
Measurements completed 1 November 2026. Publication update: 2 November 2026, Europe/Warsaw.

A small reader selects the recent internal activity of a frozen Qwen3-8B language model, compresses the selected content into a 32-number summary and updates an eight-number persistent state. A slower habit changes the selection map. A learned predictor estimates how this copy's selection differs from an ordinary average of the recent window, and its prediction helps steer the next query. The query has 256 numerical features arranged in four attention heads; these are not 256 identified concepts.

Recorded mode gives copies the same saved model activity after different warm-ups, separating developed reading habits from continuing input differences. Live mode additionally writes selected content before model layer 16 and reads the processed result after layer 24. The explorer draws these architectures separately and lets visitors inspect each module and feedback route.

Exchanging developed copies' learned predictors makes their readings more alike; restoring their original predictors often partially repairs the difference. The prediction participates in the developed way of reading. Simple private running-average controls preserve much organization, so this ownership-sensitive intervention does not uniquely require a detailed self-model.

On the same native model context, content-aligned actions influence next-token probabilities more than equally sized noise or rotated actions. Information-driven recurrent replacements also retain substantial influence through the same interface. Those comparisons distinguish structured action from effects specific to learned self-prediction. Reference action and query magnitudes are yoked in the recurrent controls; these are not completely independent replacements of the full system.

A counterbalanced information test uses eight task families, two relevant facts, two wordings and two answer-label orders: 64 presentations. Across four copies the full controller changes one of 256 choices, while more broadly softening existing answer preferences. A simple scaling account fitted on other families explains about 59% of squared answer-margin changes on held-out families. Replacing the entire selection query produces a different profile. This concerns the tested label margins, not proof that every generated response is only a temperature change.

The public explorer includes explained plots, matched response comparisons across tasks, longer development histories, architecture rationale and three synchronized paths through measured internal signals. Display projections and moving points are not named mental faculties. Exploratory semantic ratings are model-based and not human-validated; the counterbalanced label test uses direct probabilities. General personality, recognized causal ownership and subjective experience are not established.

Earlier self-description training, frozen J-space feedback, reasoning-segment memory, evidence selection and multimodal studies remain historical experiments with distinct mechanisms. They are preserved in the research repository, not presented as independent replications of the current reader.
